meta_title: Differentiation Cheat Sheet: Rules + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Master every differentiation rule with our cheat sheet, then test yourself with a free 8-question quiz on power, product, quotient and chain rules.

quiz.title: Differentiation Rules Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on the core rules and standard derivatives every Class 11-12 and competitive student needs cold. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: Using the power rule, what is d/dx (x<sup>5</sup>)?
questions.explanation: The power rule gives d/dx (x<sup>n</sup>) = n·x<sup>n−1</sup>. With n = 5 that is 5x<sup>4</sup>.

questions.q: By the product rule, d/dx (x<sup>2</sup> sin x) equals which of these?
questions.explanation: Product rule: (uv)' = u'v + uv'. Here u = x<sup>2</sup> (u' = 2x) and v = sin x (v' = cos x), giving 2x sin x + x<sup>2</sup> cos x.

questions.q: Using the quotient rule, what is d/dx (sin x / x)?
questions.explanation: Quotient rule: (u/v)' = (u'v − uv') / v<sup>2</sup>. With u = sin x, v = x this is (x cos x − sin x) / x<sup>2</sup>.

questions.q: Applying the chain rule, what is d/dx (e<sup>2x</sup>)?
questions.explanation: Chain rule: d/dx e<sup>u</sup> = e<sup>u</sup>·u'. With u = 2x, u' = 2, so the derivative is 2e<sup>2x</sup>.

questions.q: What is the derivative of tan x?
questions.explanation: d/dx (tan x) = sec<sup>2</sup> x. It follows from the quotient rule applied to sin x / cos x.

questions.q: What is the derivative of ln x (for x > 0)?
questions.explanation: d/dx (ln x) = 1/x. This is a standard result you should know without deriving it each time.
d/dx (a<sup>x</sup>) = a<sup>x</sup> ln a. The e<sup>x</sup> case is just a = e, where ln e = 1, giving back e<sup>x</sup>.

questions.q: What is the derivative of sin<sup>−1</sup> x (arcsin x)?
questions.explanation: d/dx (sin<sup>−1</sup> x) = 1 / √(1 − x<sup>2</sup>), valid for −1 < x < 1. Note cos<sup>−1</sup> x is the negative of this.

faq.q: When should I use the product rule instead of the chain rule?
faq.a: Use the product rule when two functions are multiplied, like x<sup>2</sup> sin x. Use the chain rule when one function is composed inside another, like sin(x<sup>2</sup>). Many problems need both, applied one step at a time.

faq.q: How do I remember the quotient rule?
faq.a: A common mnemonic is 'low d-high minus high d-low, over low squared': (u/v)' = (u'v − uv') / v<sup>2</sup>. Keep the order of the numerator terms right, because subtraction is not commutative.

faq.q: Why is the derivative of e<sup>x</sup> just e<sup>x</sup>?
faq.a: Because e is the unique base where the exponential function equals its own rate of change. For a general base, d/dx (a<sup>x</sup>) = a<sup>x</sup> ln a, and ln e = 1, so the ln factor vanishes.

faq.q: Which standard derivatives should I memorise for board and entrance exams?
faq.a: At minimum: the power rule, derivatives of sin, cos and tan, e<sup>x</sup>, a<sup>x</sup>, ln x, and the inverse trig functions. Knowing these instantly frees you to focus on the harder parts of a question.
